KPMG is facing international intervention as its chief executive resigns and legal loopholes limit ASIC’s access to documents and capacity to penalise the company.

Six years ago, Brendan Lyon blew the whistle on conflicts of interest and a potential multibillion-dollar hole in the New South Wales state budget while working at KPMG.

Five people directly involved in the case were later promoted at KPMG. One of them, Andrew Yates, was forced to step down immediately as chief executive on May 29 over a different scandal.

“You can’t say the circus is different when the clowns are the same,” Lyon, who is now a professor at the University of Wollongong, tells The Saturday Paper.

“The organisation, when I was there, was amoral. All of the people who refused to change that amorality became very senior leadership, partially off the back of all of the money they got in profit from those kind of exercises.”

KPMG is now facing intervention by its powerful international governing body after new allegations of conflicts of interest and corporate misconduct were made in parliament.

The scandal has put at risk strategically important work KPMG does auditing the books of some of Australia’s top companies. It raises further questions about the extraordinarily lucrative stream of government and university consulting work enjoyed by the accounting giants and the legal loophole it and the other big firms use to avoid scrutiny by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

A parliamentary inquiry has heard allegations KPMG used information that should have been kept confidential to win audit contracts at some of Australia’s biggest companies.

According to one allegation, confidential information about property giant Dexus was left open on a laptop where it could be seen by members of a separate team bidding to win the company’s audit contract.

A whistleblower has also made allegations that data from long-time audit client Lendlease was used to bid for the audit roles at Dexus and Westpac – and that their attempts to report misconduct to management were initially rebuffed.

KPMG’s turn in the spotlight comes amid increased scrutiny of the outsized role in corporate Australia and the public service of the big four accounting firms – KPMG, PwC, Deloitte and EY. It follows the long-running scandal in which PwC was caught providing advice on tax laws to the government at the same time as it coached companies on how to dodge them.

The claims against KPMG, revealed under parliamentary privilege by Labor’s Senator Deborah O’Neill and the Greens’ Senator Barbara Pocock over the past month, reached a climax last week when the firm admitted its initial internal investigations “lacked rigour”. Yates and the firm’s head of audit, Julian McPherson, both resigned.

On Wednesday, chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett stood down, although she remains a partner. Dexus refused to have her sign off its financial accounts.

KPMG promises to reinvestigate the whistleblower’s allegations and “rebuild trust” with the community.

KPMG International, the global network that allows the Australian group to trade under the prestigious name, has become involved in the local firm’s woes. A KPMG International spokesperson says all members were required to work to its standards and it took the situation in Australia seriously.

“KPMG International will continue to support the Australian firm as it rebuilds trust with its people and among its clients and communities,” the spokesperson says.

The latest scandal involves allegations of misconduct within the audit division, which is responsible for checking the financial probity of Australia’s biggest companies.

It has rocked confidence in KPMG among corporate Australia.

“The organisation, when I was there, was amoral. All of the people who refused to change that amorality became very senior leadership, partially off the back of all of the money they got in profit from those kind of exercises.”

A source with knowledge of the Dexus case says the main problem was not the information said to have been shared, thought to be relatively low-value data about KPMG’s billing for work done at the property group. Rather, it was KPMG’s failure to properly investigate the whistleblower’s allegations.

“If they’re not doing the right thing internally, how can they be doing the right thing externally?” the source tells The Saturday Paper.

Lyon says blowing the whistle at KPMG came at huge personal cost, leaving him feeling isolated and shunned by people he had thought were his colleagues. He suspects the new whistleblower is going through the same pain.

“It’s been nearly seven years of my life,” Lyon says. “It is incredibly life-changing to challenge the system. I’ve got so much respect for the current whistleblower and the way they’ve conducted themselves.”

At accounting firms, the flow of confidential and commercially sensitive client information between teams is supposed to be stopped by so-called “Chinese walls”.

Lyon says that in his time at KPMG he saw no sign they existed – and pointed to evidence he gave to the NSW parliament showing senior executives in KPMG tried to “override client confidentiality”.

“When they asked about the existence of Chinese walls, I said they must be Japanese, because they’re extremely porous and very papery,” he says.

Despite consulting’s well-known problems, governments and universities continue to rely on the sector for advice and financial oversight.

Last year, KPMG was tapped by the University of Technology Sydney for a $4.8 million review to help plan $100 million in staff cuts – a move that prompted an investigation into “psychosocial harms” by the NSW workplace safety regulator.

Tender data compiled by The Saturday Paper shows that over the past decade, KPMG has won federal government contracts worth almost $3 billion.

Lyon says a hollowed out and politicised public sector relies on the Big Four to do work it should be doing – and to dodge accountability for it.

“They talk about evidence-based decision-making, but in practice the Big Four provide decision-based evidence-making, where they will come back and evidence anything that government wants to do, whether it’s robodebt, Snowy Hydro or NBN Co,” he says. “What they do is serve a market for excuses.”

Lyon says that at the same time as the Big Four help politicians and bureaucrats avoid accountability, the firms also dodge any accountability for themselves by using partnership structures.

This means they don’t pay tax and aren’t subject to the same rules about corporate conduct and dealing properly with whistleblowers that govern their clients.

Most partnerships are limited to 20 people, with each individual partner liable for the wrongdoing of any other partner.

The big professional partnerships are exempt from the cap, however, and professional liability laws limit the amount that can be clawed back from individual partners for misconduct at the firm.

Lyon says the Big Four should be forced to become corporations.

“The reality is that we already have a mechanism to oversight large, profit driven associations of people, and they are called corporations,” he says. “They’re regulated via thousands of pages of corporations law that’s developed over the last couple of centuries.”

Barbara Pocock agrees.

“The partnership model is completely broken,” she tells The Saturday Paper.

“They have lost their social licence to say they are special and they should have special let-outs. How many of these massive scandals do we have to see before we take them at their word, which is that they’re not to be trusted?”

Last week ASIC deputy chair Sarah Court, who took control of the regulator on Monday, told federal parliament it is investigating KPMG and has already used its powers to demand documents from the audit partners at the centre of the scandal.

ASIC only has jurisdiction to investigate the auditors, however, and not the wider partnership. It cannot fine partnerships or use its sweeping investigatory powers on them and instead relies on engagement and what Court describes as “moral suasion to rein in their excesses”.

“We do think there is a gap in the regulatory oversight of large partnership models,” Court told the hearing.

ASIC faces a battle with KPMG when it comes to getting its hands on the paperwork it has been able to demand. The firm says many documents are protected from disclosure because they are correspondence with lawyers, which means they can be kept from the regulator under the principle of legal professional privilege.

Senator O’Neill tells The Saturday Paper that PwC abused legal professional privilege in its tax scandal and KPMG should not do the same.

“It would be outrageous for them to claim legal professional privilege,” she says.

“Do not cost the Australian taxpayer another cent. Give over the information immediately and do not redact one word.”

A KPMG spokesperson says the firm had proposed handing documents over in two tranches to deal with the privilege issue. The spokesperson declined to comment on Lyon’s allegations or KPMG International’s role.

Parliamentary hearings into KPMG resume on June 19.

Ben Butler is an investigative and business journalist.
